_readme: The AI Hub SQL cases: one question each, the SQL AI Hub's generator writes for it, and the
answer that SQL must come back with. This file is the only place these truths live - the
Jasmine blocks in ../sql-generation.tests.ts check the SQL text, and the AI Hub half of
GeneratedSqlAllVendorsTest runs the committed SQL of ai-hub-sql.generated.json on a throwaway
database of each vendor and compares the rows with what is written here.
A case is {id, group, proves, one of query|probe|filterPane|sql, one of rows|rowCount, ordered?,
columns?, vendors?}:
group A - cube_demo, every table schema-qualified, all nine vendors;
group B - the shipped Northwind sample and its star schema in the default schema, bare names,
the sqlite and duckdb legs;
group C - both schemas through the one connection, in the order written.
group D - the user's own SQL, sent verbatim: the generator writes nothing here. 'sql' is
one ANSI text asked of every vendor the case lists, or a map vendor -> text when
the point of the case is one database's own idiom (NVL2, LIMIT 2,2, QUALIFY...).
excluded - a vendor that refuses the construct, with the database's own error message. The
user's SQL is theirs, so a refusal is recorded here and not fixed; the loop prints
the message instead of asking the case.
vendors  - only these, when a case cannot run everywhere its group does; the reason is in
'proves'. Nothing skips silently: the loop prints every case it did not ask.
columns  - the labels AI Hub reads the row back by, compared exactly (an alias folded to
upper case by Oracle or Db2 fails).
rowCount - instead of rows where WHICH rows come back is not defined (a sample with a cap).
The answers of group A, group C's first case and group D are computed by
.docs/cube-demo-data/truths_ai_hub_cases.py into truths-ai-hub.out, from the frozen .psv rows;
they are never copied out of a product run. Group B's are Northwind's own, generated by the
product's NorthwindDataGenerator.
The generated SQL is rewritten with:
docker run --rm -v <repo>:/x -w /x/frend/reporting node:20-slim npx ts-node -r tsconfig-paths/register --project e2e/tsconfig.e2e.json e2e/explore-data/write-ai-hub-sql.ts

cases.proves: SUM and AVG in the ANSI CAST(… AS DECIMAL(31,4)) form: the average has decimals, so SQL Server's and Db2's integer division is caught
MIN and MAX of a date and of text, and COUNT DISTINCT, are not wrapped - a ROUND around them would reject a date
the plain grouped count on a qualified table - story 2's truth, and D24's
the half-open date range keeps the end day: 2025-01-08 holds 2 invoices, which a BETWEEN on a timestamp column would drop
a quote inside a contains value stays inside one literal - 7 O'Connors
a % in a contains value matches literally: 0 rows, where an unescaped % returns all 300
an _ in a contains value matches literally: 0 rows, where an unescaped _ returns all 300
a backslash in a contains value is a character, not an escape - 0 rows, and the SQL runs on MySQL, MariaDB and ClickHouse, which read \ inside a literal too
the ANSI bin form FLOOR(CAST(c AS DECIMAL(31,4)) / w) * w, over 16 bins of 25000
the row cap cuts the right two rows: the 2nd amount (351500) and the 3rd (344000) differ, so which rows a limit of 2 keeps is defined
the filter pane's value list, capped: DISTINCT, ORDER BY and the vendor's row cap (TOP after DISTINCT on SQL Server)
a filter on the flag column every vendor stores as an INTEGER: the literal is the 1 its catalog type asks for, on all nine
the month bucket and the row cap together, ordered by the bucket's own alias
the quarter label is the calendar quarter on every vendor - 7 quarters, 3000 tickets in all
hour of day on a DATE column: every row is hour 0, and Oracle's EXTRACT(HOUR FROM date) would have been rejected outright
the ISO week at the year edge: 2025-01-01 is in 2025-W01, which the old %Y-W%W form called 2025-W00
the date probe reads its own aliases back: minv/maxv come out quoted, so Oracle and Db2 do not fold them to MINV/MAXV
the number probe, read back by the same two aliases - the bin width is a guess when they come back undefined
the cardinality probe, whose alias is the column's own name
the fingerprint sample runs at all: its cap is TOP or FETCH FIRST where LIMIT was rejected, so no column on SQL Server, Oracle or Db2 ever got a semantic hint
two filters joined with AND: 402 deals are Closed Won and 858 are at or above 13000.00, and only 274 are both, so an OR or a dropped filter is caught
`>` on a number against a value 33 deals sit exactly on, so a generator that writes <= or >= for it answers 33 rows out
`>=` on a number against a value 33 deals sit exactly on, so a generator that writes > or < for it answers 33 rows out
`<` on a number against a value 33 deals sit exactly on, so a generator that writes <= or >= for it answers 33 rows out
`<=` on a number against a value 33 deals sit exactly on, so a generator that writes > or < for it answers 33 rows out
`after` on a date column, read through dateExpr and compared with the vendor's own date literal: 6 deals close exactly on 2026-02-19, so after and on-or-after differ
`on or after` on a date column, read through dateExpr and compared with the vendor's own date literal: 6 deals close exactly on 2026-02-19, so after and on-or-after differ
`before` on a date column, read through dateExpr and compared with the vendor's own date literal: 6 deals close exactly on 2026-02-19, so after and on-or-after differ
`on or before` on a date column, read through dateExpr and compared with the vendor's own date literal: 6 deals close exactly on 2026-02-19, so after and on-or-after differ
IN with a list of quoted values, split from the one box the user types them in
NOT IN with the same list: the complement, 554 of the 1200 deals
NOT IN on a column with NULLs: the 41 tickets with no agent answer neither true nor false, so 2691 of the 2959 tickets that have one come back and the NULLs are not counted
IS NULL asks the raw column, never the dateExpr wrapper: on SQLite that CASE answers a value for a NULL row, which would count 0 instead of 554
IS NOT NULL on the same temporal column: the other 646 deals
the ANSI `<>`: 798 deals are not Closed Won. `!=` is understood by all nine but is not standard SQL
COUNT of a column beside COUNT(*): 646 deals have a close_date and 1200 rows exist, so a COUNT(column) written as COUNT(*) is caught
an empty value box asks nothing (Q2): `in` with nothing typed has always written 1=1, and still answers every deal
an empty value box asks nothing (Q2): `=` with nothing typed is left out of the WHERE, where it used to filter to the rows whose stage is the empty string - 0 of them
an empty value box asks nothing (Q2): `>` with nothing typed is left out of the WHERE, where PostgreSQL and SQL Server used to reject the query outright
`starts with` folds the case like `contains`: `closed` finds the 646 Closed Won and Closed Lost deals, where the old `stage LIKE 'closed%'` found 0 on PostgreSQL, Oracle, Db2, DuckDB and ClickHouse
`starts with` escapes the wildcards the user types: a `%` is the character, and no stage holds one - unescaped it matched every row, 1200
`ends with` folds the case too: `won` finds the 402 Closed Won deals, and the % sits at the front of the pattern, not the end
`ends with` escapes `_`, the LIKE wildcard for one character: no stage ends with a literal underscore, where unescaped it matched all 1200

NULLs sort last, ascending: 554 of the 1200 deals have no close date, so the three rows a limit of 3 keeps are the three earliest dated deals - MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and SQLite sort NULLs first ascending and would show three deals with no close date at all

NULLs sort last, descending too: PostgreSQL, Oracle, Db2, DuckDB and ClickHouse sort NULLs first descending and would show three deals with no close date; these three are the latest dated deals, tied on 2026-09-30 and split by deal_id

top N of an aggregated query: the sort key is the aggregate, and it is written as COUNT(*) - the alias PostgreSQL rejects inside an ORDER BY expression - so the three biggest stages come back in that order on all nine, SQL Server through TOP

the weekday is 0..6 with Sunday 0 on all nine, and no session setting moves it: SQL Server cancels SET DATEFIRST with @@DATEFIRST, Oracle counts from the Monday of the ISO week (ISO weeks start on Monday whatever NLS_TERRITORY says) and Db2 uses DAYOFWEEK, where 1 is Sunday by definition - the case is asked twice on SQL Server and Oracle, once in the loop's own session and once under the hostile one named below, and must answer the same both times
the day bucket is the same sortable yyyy-mm-dd label on all nine, so a limit of 5 takes the five earliest days and not five days of some other order
the year bucket is the four-digit year, the same two rows on all nine
the month of the year is a number 1..12 - the month ACROSS the years, which is not the '2025-01' label the month bucket writes
the quarter of the year is a number 1..4, again across the years

a relative date filter is a computed range of whole days: `in the last 3 months` with today = 2026-09-30 is close_date >= 2026-07-01 and < 2026-10-01, the same ANSI range on all nine (no CURRENT_DATE, no interval), and 67 of the 646 dated deals fall in it

COUNT DISTINCT, the aggregate the Summarize step now offers: 3000 orders were placed by 359 different customers, and the 240 orders with no customer_id are not counted as a customer on any of the nine

a computed column, the canvas's first use case: `line_revenue = unit_price x qty` over the 5500 invoice lines sums to 20411515.04, which is exactly the SUM of the `amount` column the table already carries - the same ANSI `(a * b)` on all nine, inside the DECIMAL(31,4) cast a SUM has always had

a computed division: dividing by zero answers NULL instead of failing the query (NULLIF), so the 5957 of 8500 order lines whose discount is 0 are simply not counted and 2543 are; and the DECIMAL cast keeps the decimals - every one of the 8500 lines has half a qty above zero, where the integer division PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite and Db2 do without the cast would answer only the 4601 lines of two or more

a condition on an aggregate: `HAVING COUNT(*) > 150` keeps the three stages of more than 150 deals and drops the other three, which no WHERE can express - the count exists only once the rows are grouped; the same ANSI HAVING on all nine, holding the aggregate expression and not its alias

two conditions joined with AND, one of them on a SUM inside its DECIMAL(31,4) cast: only Closed Won has both more than 150 deals and more than 10 million of amount - Closed Lost passes the count with 244 deals and fails the money with 9037500

matching ANY filter rather than all of them: `stage = 'Closed Won' OR amount > 80000` answers 474 deals, where the same two filters joined with AND answer 27 - the OR set stands inside one pair of brackets, so the five stages that are not Closed Won keep only their big deals

grouping with nothing to summarize is a question of its own - which combinations are there - and it is `SELECT DISTINCT stage`: the 6 stages of 1200 deals, not the 1200 rows the grouping used to be dropped into

an aggregate read as a % of the whole result: each stage's money over the money of every stage, `100.0 * SUM(amount) / NULLIF(SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (), 0)` - the total is a number no grouped row holds, so it is a window over the grouped rows, and the six shares add up to 100

an aggregate accumulated up to its bucket: the monthly count of closed deals and the deals closed so far, `SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (ORDER BY <month bucket> ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)` - the accumulation runs in the bucket's own order, and the 554 deals with no close date are one bucket of their own at the END of the series (T6), where the running total reaches all 1200
a Date dashboard parameter is bound as a date, not as the text it arrives as: the same comparison bound as text is an error on PostgreSQL and the wrong rows on SQLite

excluded.clickhouse: java.sql.SQLException: Code: 53. DB::Exception: Cannot convert string 2026-01-31 14:05:00 to type Date32. (TYPE_MISMATCH) (version 24.3.18.7 (official build))

cases.proves: a DateTime parameter arrives in the datetime-local form, with the seconds left out, and is bound as a timestamp; a date column read at midnight answers p1a's count; ClickHouse is the one database that will not read a timestamp against a date column at all - its Date32 refuses the binding outright, and that refusal is recorded
an Integer parameter is bound as a number, so a numeric column is not compared with a string
a Double parameter keeps its fraction: 31999.99 holds the nine deals of exactly 32000.00 that the Integer 32000 cuts

a dashboard date range bound to two Date parameters answers exactly what a4 answers with the same two days typed in, 18: the range ends on the day after `to`, and that day is derived where the value is bound (DateParameters), named in the SQL as a parameter of its own and never computed in SQL - ended at `to` itself the count is 16, the 2 invoices of 2025-01-08 dropped

`on or before` a Date parameter is the whole day as well: every invoice up to the end of 2025-01-08, which is the same 18 - the form it had before, `<= ${to}`, is the instant at midnight and drops that day's 2 invoices on a column that holds a time
a bare table name with a space, and the ANSI AVG: 10.7254, where integer division gives 10
MIN and MAX of a DECIMAL column, unwrapped
SUM and AVG over 7937 rows of the star schema, on FLOAT and DECIMAL columns
a bin width of 0.1 prints as 0.1 - never 0.30000000000000004 or 1e-7 - and bins a FLOAT column
the month bucket on Northwind's own OrderDate, which SQLite's JDBC sample stores as epoch ms
the row cap on a bare table, ordered by the aggregate's alias
the filter pane on a mixed-case column of a bare table
a quote in a contains value on data nobody invented: Bon app'

the date probe on a column stored as a real date - the aliases come back as asked. Asked on duckdb only: SQLite's Northwind stores OrderDate as epoch ms, and NorthwindFixture writes those rows at LOCAL midnight, so the calendar day the vendor layer reads back with 'unixepoch' (UTC) depends on the JVM's time zone - it is 2022-12-04 in a UTC+14 zone. The epoch decoding itself is proven as text in Jasmine block 9, and the date probe runs on the sqlite leg in a14-probe-date-range, whose column the seed script stores as a DATE
the number probe on a bare table
the cardinality probe on a mixed-case column
the qualified table on a connection that also holds the default schema: story 13's total
the bare table right after it, on the same connection: qualifying one table changed nothing about the other
OR inside brackets, AND outside: the brackets are the user's and nothing moves them
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE (stage = 'Closed Won' OR stage = 'Closed Lost')
  AND amount > 20000

cases.proves: SELECT DISTINCT, the plain ANSI form every database has
cases.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT stage
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
ORDER BY stage

cases.proves: arithmetic on a column inside the condition
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE amount * 2 > 64000

cases.proves: CASE WHEN, grouped by the expression itself - an alias in GROUP BY is not portable, and the user's SQL is not rewritten to make it so
cases.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN amount >= 30000 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END AS deal_size, count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
GROUP BY CASE WHEN amount >= 30000 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END
ORDER BY deal_size

cases.proves: COALESCE over a NULL date column
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE COALESCE(close_date, DATE '2030-01-01') > DATE '2026-06-30'

excluded.sqlite: org.sqlite.SQLiteException: [SQLITE_ERROR] SQL error or missing database (near "'2030-01-01'": syntax error)

cases.proves: NULLIF turns one value into nothing, and IS NULL finds it
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE NULLIF(stage, 'Closed Won') IS NULL

cases.proves: HAVING, a condition on an aggregate
cases.sql:
SELECT stage, count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
GROUP BY stage
HAVING count(*) > 200
ORDER BY stage

cases.proves: IN (SELECT ...), a subquery in the condition
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE account_id IN (SELECT account_id FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts WHERE country = 'Germany')

cases.proves: EXISTS with a correlated subquery - the same question as d8-in-subquery, so the two must answer the same number
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals d
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts a
              WHERE a.account_id = d.account_id AND a.country = 'Germany')

excluded.clickhouse: java.sql.SQLException: Code: 1. DB::Exception: Resolve identifier 'd.account_id' from parent scope only supported for constants and CTE. Actual d.account_id node type COLUMN. (UNSUPPORTED_METHOD) (version 24.3.18.7 (official build))

cases.proves: a CTE (WITH), and SELECT * inside it
cases.sql:
WITH won AS (SELECT * FROM cube_demo.crm_deals WHERE stage = 'Closed Won')
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count, sum(amount) AS total
FROM won

cases.proves: ROW_NUMBER and RANK in a subquery, filtered by the row number
cases.sql:
SELECT stage, n, rn, rk
FROM (SELECT stage, count(*) AS n,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC, stage) AS rn,
             RANK() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC) AS rk
      FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
      GROUP BY stage) t
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY rn

cases.proves: a running SUM over a window, the everyday cumulative line
cases.sql:
SELECT stage, n, SUM(n) OVER (ORDER BY stage) AS running
FROM (SELECT stage, count(*) AS n FROM cube_demo.crm_deals GROUP BY stage) t
ORDER BY stage

cases.proves: UNION ALL over two tables, with an ORDER BY on the union
cases.sql:
SELECT 'accounts' AS what, count(*) AS n FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts
UNION ALL
SELECT 'deals' AS what, count(*) AS n FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
ORDER BY what

cases.proves: UPPER and TRIM in the condition
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS account_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts
WHERE UPPER(TRIM(country)) = 'GERMANY'

cases.proves: the ANSI substring form, SUBSTRING(x FROM 1 FOR 3) - a vendor that refuses it is recorded in `excluded`, not fixed
cases.sql:
SELECT count(DISTINCT SUBSTRING(name FROM 1 FOR 3)) AS prefixes
FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts

excluded.sqlite: org.sqlite.SQLiteException: [SQLITE_ERROR] SQL error or missing database (near "FROM": syntax error)

cases.proves: CAST to DECIMAL and to VARCHAR in one condition
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(12,2)) > 31999.99
  AND CAST(deal_id AS VARCHAR(20)) LIKE '1%'

excluded.mysql: java.sql.SQLSyntaxErrorException: You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version for the right syntax to use near 'VARCHAR(20)) LIKE '1%'' at line 4

cases.proves: OFFSET ... FETCH, the ANSI paging form - MySQL and SQLite have LIMIT instead, and their refusal is recorded; MariaDB answers it
cases.sql:
SELECT stage, count(*) AS n
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
GROUP BY stage
ORDER BY n DESC, stage
OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 2 ROWS ONLY

excluded.sqlite: org.sqlite.SQLiteException: [SQLITE_ERROR] SQL error or missing database (near "OFFSET": syntax error)
excluded.mysql: java.sql.SQLSyntaxErrorException: You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version for the right syntax to use near 'OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 2 ROWS ONLY' at line 5

cases.proves: interval arithmetic on a date written out in full, so the answer cannot move with the clock
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > DATE '2026-09-30' - INTERVAL '30' DAY

excluded.sqlite: org.sqlite.SQLiteException: [SQLITE_ERROR] SQL error or missing database (near "'2026-09-30'": syntax error)
excluded.db2: com.ibm.db2.jcc.am.SqlSyntaxErrorException: DB2 SQL Error: SQLCODE=-105, SQLSTATE=42604, SQLERRMC=30, DRIVER=4.35.11

cases.proves: a `:` and a `?` inside a string literal reach the database as typed: JDBI must not read them as binds
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE stage <> 'a:b' AND deal_name NOT LIKE '%?%'

cases.proves: Oracle NVL, NVL2 and DECODE: the null-handling and conditional idioms an Oracle user writes every day

sql.oracle:
SELECT SUM(NVL2(close_date, 0, 1)) AS still_open,
       SUM(NVL2(close_date, 1, 0)) AS closed,
       COUNT(DECODE(stage, 'Closed Won', 1, NULL)) AS won,
       COUNT(NVL(close_date, DATE '2030-01-01')) AS all_deals
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: Oracle ADD_MONTHS, TO_DATE, TRUNC and SYSDATE - the clock only in a comparison whose answer cannot move

sql.oracle:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > ADD_MONTHS(TO_DATE('2026-09-30', 'YYYY-MM-DD'), -1)
  AND TRUNC(SYSDATE) > TO_DATE('2000-01-01', 'YYYY-MM-DD')

cases.proves: Oracle LISTAGG ... WITHIN GROUP

sql.oracle:
SELECT LISTAGG(stage, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY stage) AS stages
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT stage FROM cube_demo.crm_deals)

cases.proves: Oracle ROWNUM, the paging idiom from before 12c

sql.oracle:
SELECT count(*) AS first_ten
FROM (SELECT deal_id FROM cube_demo.crm_deals WHERE ROWNUM <= 10)

cases.proves: Oracle's (+) outer join, written the old way

sql.oracle:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals d, cube_demo.crm_accounts a
WHERE d.account_id = a.account_id(+)
  AND a.country = 'Germany'

cases.proves: MySQL/MariaDB IF() and IFNULL(), the everyday conditional and null-handling forms

sql.mysql:
SELECT SUM(IF(close_date IS NULL, 1, 0)) AS still_open,
       SUM(IF(IFNULL(close_date, '2030-01-01') > '2026-06-30', 0, 1)) AS closed_before_july
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
sql.mariadb:
SELECT SUM(IF(close_date IS NULL, 1, 0)) AS still_open,
       SUM(IF(IFNULL(close_date, '2030-01-01') > '2026-06-30', 0, 1)) AS closed_before_july
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: MySQL/MariaDB DATE_SUB(... INTERVAL ...) and NOW(), the clock only where it cannot move the answer

sql.mysql:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > DATE_SUB(DATE '2026-09-30', INTERVAL 31 DAY)
  AND NOW() > DATE '2000-01-01'
sql.mariadb:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > DATE_SUB(DATE '2026-09-30', INTERVAL 31 DAY)
  AND NOW() > DATE '2000-01-01'

cases.proves: MySQL/MariaDB GROUP_CONCAT with its own ORDER BY and SEPARATOR

sql.mysql:
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT stage ORDER BY stage SEPARATOR ',') AS stages
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
sql.mariadb:
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT stage ORDER BY stage SEPARATOR ',') AS stages
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: MySQL/MariaDB `LIMIT offset, count` - the paging form no other database has

sql.mysql:
SELECT stage, count(*) AS n
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
GROUP BY stage
ORDER BY n DESC, stage
LIMIT 2, 2
sql.mariadb:
SELECT stage, count(*) AS n
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
GROUP BY stage
ORDER BY n DESC, stage
LIMIT 2, 2

cases.proves: MariaDB's own ROWNUM() (10.6+) and LIMIT ... ROWS EXAMINED

sql.mariadb:
SELECT deal_id
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE ROWNUM() <= 3
ORDER BY deal_id
LIMIT 3 ROWS EXAMINED 5000

cases.proves: SQL Server ISNULL and DATEDIFF

sql.sqlserver:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN ISNULL(close_date, '2030-01-01') > '2026-06-30' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS later,
       DATEDIFF(day, '2026-08-30', '2026-09-30') AS days
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: SQL Server DATEADD and GETDATE(), the clock only in a comparison whose answer cannot move

sql.sqlserver:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > DATEADD(day, -31, CAST('2026-09-30' AS date))
  AND GETDATE() > CAST('2000-01-01' AS date)

cases.proves: SQL Server CONVERT with style 23 and STRING_AGG ... WITHIN GROUP

sql.sqlserver:
SELECT CONVERT(varchar, CAST('2026-09-30' AS date), 23) AS the_day,
       STRING_AGG(s.stage, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY s.stage) AS stages
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT stage FROM cube_demo.crm_deals) s

cases.proves: SQL Server TOP, CROSS APPLY and WITH (NOLOCK) together

sql.sqlserver:
SELECT TOP 2 a.city, x.employees
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT city FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts WITH (NOLOCK) WHERE country = 'Germany') a
CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 b.employees FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts b
             WHERE b.city = a.city AND b.country = 'Germany'
             ORDER BY b.employees DESC) x
ORDER BY a.city

cases.proves: PostgreSQL's :: casts and ILIKE

sql.postgres:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
        WHERE amount::numeric > 31999.99 AND deal_id::text LIKE '1%') AS cast_count,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts WHERE country ILIKE 'germany') AS ilike_count

cases.proves: PostgreSQL date_trunc and now() - INTERVAL, the month bucket of a written-out date

sql.postgres:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date >= date_trunc('month', DATE '2026-09-30')
  AND close_date < date_trunc('month', DATE '2026-09-30') + INTERVAL '1 month'
  AND now() - INTERVAL '1 day' > TIMESTAMP '2000-01-01'

cases.proves: PostgreSQL FILTER (WHERE ...) and string_agg with its own ORDER BY

sql.postgres:
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE stage = 'Closed Won') AS won,
       string_agg(DISTINCT stage, ',' ORDER BY stage) AS stages
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON: the largest account of each German city

sql.postgres:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (city) city, name, employees
FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts
WHERE country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY city, employees DESC

cases.proves: PostgreSQL generate_series, a table function in the FROM

sql.postgres: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM generate_series(1, 10)

cases.proves: Db2 CURRENT DATE and labeled durations (`d - 31 DAYS`)

sql.db2:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > DATE('2026-09-30') - 31 DAYS
  AND CURRENT DATE > DATE('2000-01-01')

cases.proves: Db2 VALUE() (its COALESCE) and LISTAGG

sql.db2:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
        WHERE VALUE(close_date, DATE('2030-01-01')) > DATE('2026-06-30')) AS later,
       (SELECT LISTAGG(stage, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY stage)
        FROM (SELECT DISTINCT stage FROM cube_demo.crm_deals) t) AS stages
FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1

cases.proves: Db2 VALUES as a table, and the WITH UR isolation clause

sql.db2: SELECT count(*) AS n FROM (VALUES (1), (2), (3)) AS t(n) WITH UR

cases.proves: SQLite's date modifiers, date(d, '-31 days')

sql.sqlite:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > date('2026-09-30', '-31 days')

cases.proves: SQLite julianday arithmetic

sql.sqlite:
SELECT CAST(julianday('2026-09-30') - julianday('2026-08-30') AS INTEGER) AS days
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals LIMIT 1

cases.proves: SQLite IFNULL and the || concatenation

sql.sqlite:
SELECT count(*) AS won
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE IFNULL(stage, '') || '!' = 'Closed Won!'

cases.proves: SQLite group_concat and rowid

sql.sqlite:
SELECT (SELECT group_concat(stage, ',') FROM (SELECT DISTINCT stage FROM cube_demo.crm_deals ORDER BY stage)) AS stages,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT rowid FROM cube_demo.crm_deals LIMIT 10)) AS first_ten

cases.proves: DuckDB GROUP BY ALL

sql.duckdb:
SELECT stage, count(*) AS n
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY stage

cases.proves: DuckDB SELECT * EXCLUDE and QUALIFY

sql.duckdb:
SELECT count(*) AS one_per_stage
FROM (SELECT * EXCLUDE (deal_name)
      FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
      QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY stage ORDER BY deal_id) = 1) t

cases.proves: DuckDB date_trunc and ILIKE

sql.duckdb:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
        WHERE close_date >= date_trunc('month', DATE '2026-09-30')) AS september,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts WHERE country ILIKE 'germany') AS german

cases.proves: DuckDB strptime, reading a date out of text

sql.duckdb:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > strptime('2026-08-30', '%Y-%m-%d')

cases.proves: ClickHouse toDate arithmetic and today(), the clock only where it cannot move the answer

sql.clickhouse:
SELECT count(*) AS deal_count
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE close_date > toDate('2026-09-30') - 31
  AND today() > toDate('2000-01-01')

cases.proves: ClickHouse toStartOfMonth and dateDiff

sql.clickhouse:
SELECT countIf(close_date >= toStartOfMonth(toDate('2026-09-30'))) AS september,
       dateDiff('day', toDate('2026-08-30'), toDate('2026-09-30')) AS days
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: ClickHouse uniqExact, its exact COUNT DISTINCT

sql.clickhouse:
SELECT uniqExact(stage) AS stages, uniqExact(account_id) AS accounts
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals

cases.proves: ClickHouse LIMIT 1 BY: the largest account of each German city

sql.clickhouse:
SELECT city, employees
FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts
WHERE country = 'Germany'
ORDER BY city, employees DESC
LIMIT 1 BY city

cases.proves: ClickHouse argMax and PREWHERE

sql.clickhouse:
SELECT argMax(name, employees) AS largest
FROM cube_demo.crm_accounts
PREWHERE country = 'Germany'

cases.proves: the label a database gives an unquoted alias: Oracle and Db2 fold `n` to `N`, the other seven answer `n` - recorded per vendor, not quoted away, because the SQL is the user's
cases.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS n
FROM cube_demo.crm_deals
WHERE stage = 'Closed Won'

cases.proves: DuckDB PIVOT: one row, a column per stage, the stage names themselves as labels

sql.duckdb: PIVOT (SELECT stage FROM cube_demo.crm_deals) ON stage USING count(*)
